money_at_stake.rationale: The occurrence's own claim names a mutiny plus a decree reallocating the Orano and GoviEx uranium permits, so the tightest, most directly attributable pool is Niger's own uranium production and export revenue, not the global nuclear-fuel-cycle market the sector sits inside. That pool is small and shrinking: Niger's uranium/thorium ore exports were USD 204.36 million in 2023 (up from USD 134 million in 2022), and mine production has since collapsed to 962 tU in 2024, about 1.6% of world output, down from 2,020 tU in 2022 (the last full year before the 2023 coup and the SOMAIR/GoviEx expropriations that preceded this occurrence). At the current spot price of USD 89.85/lb U3O8, even Niger's full pre-disruption output would convert to well under half a billion dollars a year, not a hundred. I deliberately did NOT band on the global front-end nuclear fuel cycle (conversion, enrichment, fabrication), which published market-research estimates put in the tens of billions annually: that is Nell's named unmapped chain layer, but it is a structural industry TAM that exists independent of this occurrence, not money this specific mutiny-and-permit event moves. Using it would be exactly the reasoned-but-unattached number method section 0.2 refuses.

public_reach.rationale: This corrects the candidate card's framing rather than confirming it. The card's claim, and Nell's 'why' note, describe both reallocated permits landing on state-backed companies with the reachable set confined to conversion, enrichment and fuel-fabrication names 'behind the miners.' Independent verification shows that is only half true. Orano's former asset (the In Azaoua permit at Arlit, ex-SOMAIR) did go entirely to TSUMCO SA, a company created by and wholly owned by the Nigerien state: zero listed reach there, confirming the card. But the GoviEx asset (the Madaouela permit) did NOT go to a state-backed company. On 2026-08-21 Niger's Council of Ministers re-granted it to MAMICO, a new Nigerien subsidiary in which Atomic Eagle Ltd, a genuine ASX-listed developer (ticker AEU, trading since 18 November 2025), holds 60% and operational control, with the Nigerien state holding the other 40% (a 15% free-carry plus a 25% contributing stake). GoviEx, the very entity the occurrence's own claim names as expropriated, is now itself an Atomic Eagle subsidiary, so the 'GoviEx permit' and 'a listed issuer' are the same lineage, not two separate things. That is a real, current, tradeable listed touchpoint directly on a mining permit, not a second-order supplier. It does not flip the picture to REACHABLE, for three reasons that keep the score below the 40 anchor's midpoint: Madaouela is pre-production (a JORC resource is still pending in 2026, with resource verification and technical optimisation only just underway), so today's actual revenue through the listed vehicle is zero; the larger, historically revenue-generating asset (ex-SOMAIR/Arlit) is the 100%-state one; and the state extracted real terms (a USD 10 million upfront royalty from MAMICO) even from the 'listed' half. Scored at 35: a genuine minority-but-real listed channel exists on the smaller, non-producing half of the two reallocated assets, while the larger, producing half remains fully state-captured.

capture_odds.rationale: The jurisdiction has now run this exact play twice against foreign, listed-adjacent developers inside three years: Niger revoked GoviEx's Madaouela permit in 2024, and nationalized Orano's SOMAIR mine in June 2025 on the stated grounds that Orano had taken 86.3% of production against a 63% equity stake. That is a demonstrated pattern of the state re-capturing majority economics from the operator of record, not an isolated event. Atomic Eagle's 'recovery' of Madaouela is a re-entry on WORSE terms than a clean concession: 60% rather than outright ownership, a 40% state stake structured with a free-carry, and a USD 10 million upfront royalty, arriving only after GoviEx (now its own subsidiary) had already sunk capital into the project with zero return through the expropriation. Against that, uranium itself is a genuinely strengthening commodity right now (spot near USD 90/lb as of 2026-08-30), which is real upside if a project ever reaches production and the political risk does not recur. There is no production revenue today for either reallocated asset to test capture against. Scored at 25, below the 'some specs, mostly price-taker' anchor (40): this reads closer to a jurisdiction where the state resets the split whenever the asset becomes valuable, which caps what a public shareholder can expect to keep even before construction risk is added.

timing_fit.rationale: Anchored to the 2026-08-29 mutiny and the 2026-08-21 decree it followed within the same week. Niger's existing (state-captured) uranium production is already flowing now, trivially inside the 2-5 year window, but that money is not the reachable piece and does not help this leg. The reachable piece, Atomic Eagle's 60% of Madaouela, is pre-production: a JORC mineral resource was still pending as of the August 2026 mining convention, with resource verification and technical optimisation only just underway, a sequence that typically runs five or more years for a uranium project even without added risk. On top of an already slow build timeline sits acute, recurring execution risk: this is the second major disruption to Niger's uranium sector in three years (the 2023 coup, and now an armed mutiny attempt on the capital days after the permit decree was signed), and mutiny risk in this specific government has just been demonstrated live, not merely asserted. Scored near 'slipping past it' rather than 'beyond the horizon' because Atomic Eagle chose to finalize and announce its convention despite the instability, signalling the company's own base case is still inside a multi-year, not multi-decade, horizon.

notes.text: The candidate card's 'why' field scopes this away from a direct uranium-miner framing by analogy to TASTE-001, and its occurrence claim describes both reallocated permits going to 'state-backed companies.' Independent verification finds that description accurate for the Orano/TSUMCO half and inaccurate for the GoviEx/Madaouela half, which went 60% to Atomic Eagle Ltd (ASX-listed), with GoviEx now an Atomic Eagle subsidiary. TASTE-001 itself would not obviously bind a small-cap ASX developer with no documented retail-enthusiasm evidence the way it binds MP Materials or Lynas, but that is a scoping question for whoever runs the chain, not for this appraisal. What this appraisal says is narrower: THIN, because the money at stake in Niger's own uranium sector is well under a billion dollars a year and shrinking, not because no listed issuer touches it. If a chain is built here, it should start from the Atomic Eagle/Madaouela permit itself, which is a real, current, listed, exposed name, rather than assuming the whole occurrence is unreachable.
